introduction_markdown: Multiple choice paper (English Language 1, June 2021, Ordinary Level, code 0530). Answer ALL 50 questions; all questions carry equal marks. Each question has four suggested answers A, B, C and D; mark only one answer for each question. The paper has four sections: A listening comprehension (questions 1-10), B reading comprehension (questions 11-25), C grammar (questions 26-40) and D vocabulary (questions 41-50).
enonce_intro_markdown: **Multiple choice questions** - choose the one correct answer, A, B, C or D.
incertitudes: Questions ouvertes (deux options defendables) : Q5 (B was unhappy and life was joyless contre D felt nobody loved him, A felt frustrated and lonely aussi proche), Q9 (C pity contre D humility), Q13 (B common contre A collective), Q31 (B Practically everyone contre A Neither of us).

Cles retenues mais moins sures : Q3 (C stole money from the house ; le texte dit seulement qu'il devrait expliquer d'ou vient l'argent ; concurrente D private paid jobs), Q7 (B real, le 'ea' de tears /ɪə/ ; soulignement lu sur l'image), Q19 (C improve on the situation ; concurrentes A et D), Q24 (A intermediate technology ; concurrente D create more work places), Q28 (B call ; concurrente C call for), Q41 (C most ; concurrentes D many et A some).

Le sujet imprime 'You head the word tears' a la Q7 (faute pour heard) ; recopie corrigee en 'heard'. Le texte du passage 2 emploie 'work places' dans l'enonce de la Q22 et 'workplaces' dans le texte ; recopies telles quelles.

Le texte de l'ecoute (Section A) vient des pages d'instructions du professeur, recopie sans les barres obliques de pause et sans les consignes de conduite. Les titres Section One/Two/Three correspondent aux questions 1-4, 5-7 et 8-10 du livret.

Le PDF est une photocopie sans couche texte. Les numeros de ligne des passages de lecture sont repris entre crochets, a la fin de la ligne imprimee ; leur position est approximative a quelques mots pres. Les mots en gras des textes sont ceux que le sujet met en gras ; les mots soulignes des questions 7 et 46 a 50 sont rendus en gras.
Q34 : options B et D imprimees daughter's-in-laws et 'daughters-in - law' ; Q40 : les options B et D n'ont qu'une seule virgule ; Q41 : l'enonce imprime 'Therefore, ____ came.' Recopies tels quels.

Les sections de grammaire (26-40) et de vocabulaire (41-50) sont recopiees avec leurs consignes ; l'en-tete de section est dans l'enonce de la Q26 et de la Q41 (consigne 'For numbers 26-38' et 'For numbers 41-45').

questions.enonce_markdown:
**Listening passage (read aloud once by the examiner in the real exam - read it once, then answer)**

**Mensa's first day in school**

**Section One**

Mensa was among the lots of boys who lined up in front of the women who sold food to the children in the canteen. He had no money but had followed the crowd. He was surprised to find that Aunt Zola was among them. Unlike the other women, Aunt Zola had more things to sell, the notable ones being rice and stew, fried plantains, fried cocoyam and sweets. She was watching Mensa to see if he would buy anything.

She knew Mensa had no money right there. If he bought anything, he would have to explain later in the house how and where he got the money. Mensa did not like the way she watched him, so, he had to withdraw from the line. He was sad and disappointed, for he had noticed soon afterwards that Aunt Zola had called her two children, who had started school with him that day, and had given them something to eat, though all of them had had breakfast before leaving for school that morning.

**Section Two**

Mensa went and sat down at a corner and for the first time since he came to live with his uncle, he wept. He felt nobody had any love for him and life was without joy. Not that he fully understood his plight, but he knew that those who loved and cared for him had sent him to a strange place, where human beings existed not for him but for others.

Mensa's face was still wet with tears when, turning his head, he noticed a boy whom he had never seen before, come to sit by him. The boy was lean, very dark and extremely handsome. His features were clean-cut. He spoke softly and asked him, "Is your name Mensa?" "Yes," he replied.

**Section Three**

"Somebody told me you were living with our head teacher, is it true?"

"Yes, it's true." "Why did you choose to live with him?" the strange boy asked.

"I don't know. It was my father who sent me to him." Mensa answered, not knowing why he had said so. Then, he asked the strange boy, "What's your name?" "Zuma," the boy told him, and smiled gently, displaying a fine set of clean white teeth. He had dimples and his face was smooth and well washed.

"Look, Mensa, I've bought more fried plantains from the headmaster's wife than I can eat. You'd better have some," Zuma said, pushing some of the fried plantain into Mensa's hand. Mensa felt unexpected warmth and from that day they became friends.

**Section A - Listening comprehension (5 marks).** Using only the material read to you from the Listening Comprehension passage, answer each of the following questions as directed. Choose the best answer from the alternatives (A, B, C and D) for each of the questions below.

**Section One**

1. Mensa was surprised because \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: Mensa had no money and had only followed the crowd. The passage says "He was surprised to find that Aunt Zola was among them", meaning among the women selling food. He had no money (A) but that is not what surprised him; he had followed the crowd (C) is a fact, not the cause of his surprise; the many varieties of food (D) are only listed. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: Aunt Zola was among the sellers
the varieties of food were many

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Listening passage above) Section One

2. When Aunt Zola saw Mensa on the line she stared at him with \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: She "was watching Mensa to see if he would buy anything" because she knew he had no money, so that anything he bought would call for an explanation. She watched him with suspicion. Anger and surprise are not mentioned, and "doubt" is weaker than the distrust the passage describes ("Mensa did not like the way she watched him"). **Answer: A.**
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Listening passage above) Section One

3. If Mensa had bought anything it would have been interpreted at home that \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: Aunt Zola knew he had no money "right there", so if he bought something "he would have to explain later in the house how and where he got the money". The only option that fits this suspicion is that he had stolen money from the house. Begging at school, secret gifts from parents and paid jobs are never suggested. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: he had begged money at school
his parents had secretly given him money
he had stolen money from the house
he had done private paid jobs

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Listening passage above) Section One

4. Mensa was sad and disappointed because \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The passage says he was sad and disappointed "for he had noticed soon afterwards that Aunt Zola had called her two children ... and had given them something to eat". So the cause was that his aunt fed her own sons while he had nothing. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: he was scared of his aunt's looks
his aunt had given food to her sons
the breakfast he had had was small

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Listening passage above) Section Two

5. In this passage, Mensa wept because he \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

*Options as printed:* A) felt frustrated and lonely   B) was unhappy and life was joyless   C) lived away from his parents   D) felt nobody loved him
questions.corrige_markdown:
The passage says "he wept. He felt nobody had any love for him and life was without joy". Option D ("felt nobody loved him") repeats the first part and option B ("was unhappy and life was joyless") repeats the second part; option A (frustrated and lonely) is a looser summary of both. Because B and D are both taken from the passage, this question is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

**Answer: B (unhappy and life was joyless) and D (felt nobody loved him) are both supported by the passage.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Listening passage above) Section Two

6. The word 'plight' read to you from the passage is closest in meaning to \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Plight" means a difficult or unfortunate situation, so the closest word is "troubles". A "dilemma" is a choice between two bad options, "confusion" is a mental state and "pressures" are forces put on someone. **Answer: A.**
themes: O Level English - synonyms and antonyms

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Listening passage above) Section Two

7. You heard the word 'tears' read to you from the passage. Which word below has the same sound as that underlined in 't**ea**rs'?
questions.corrige_markdown: In the passage "tears" means drops of water from the eyes, pronounced /tɪəz/ (TEERZ). The underlined letters 'ea' therefore have the sound /ɪə/, which is the sound of 'ea' in "real" /rɪəl/. "Heal" has /iː/, "pear" has /eə/ and "head" has /e/. **Answer: B.**
themes: O Level English - syllables and sounds

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Listening passage above) Section Three

8. Mensa had to live with the head teacher because \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: Mensa says "It was my father who sent me to him". The reason he gives is his father's wish. The other reasons (school, better learning, nowhere else to live) are never stated. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: his father wanted him to go to school
he would learn better living with him
he had nowhere else to live

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Listening passage above) Section Three

9. Zuma pushed some of his plantains into Mensa's hand as a sign of \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

*Options as printed:* A) pride   B) riches   C) pity   D) humility
questions.corrige_markdown:
Zuma had seen Mensa's tear-stained face and, pretending that he had bought more than he could eat, gave him food. This can be read as pity (he feels sorry for Mensa) or as humility (he gives without showing off or humiliating him). Pride and riches do not fit. Because pity (C) and humility (D) are both defensible, this question is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

**Answer: pity (C) is the most natural reading; humility (D) is also defensible.**
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Listening passage above) Section Three

10. The most likely moral lesson drawn from this story is that \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: Mensa is treated coldly by his aunt, while a stranger, Zuma, shows him kindness and they become friends. The lesson is that people should be nice to those they live with (and to others). The story does not say children should school near home or never leave home, and "women are very wicked" is a generalisation that the story does not support (Zuma bought the plantains from the headmaster's wife). **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: children should school near their homes
children should never leave their homes
people should be nice to those they live with
women are very wicked to relatives

questions.enonce_markdown:
**Section B - Reading comprehension (7½ marks).** Read the following passage and answer the questions which follow.

**Passage for questions 11 to 18** (the numbers in square brackets are the line numbers printed in the paper)

**Passage 1**

Books are for reading, but men must bring to their reading a desire to learn and a power to assimilate. Reading a book without assimilating it is like eating a meal without digesting it. When students first go to the library, they may be puzzled as to what to read of all the different subjects. According to Francis Bacon, a student should read books on those subjects which he is insufficiently acquainted; yet he should be selective in his reading. It is no good just trying to fill your mind with knowledge. [5] Knowledge in itself is often useless. A mind overloaded with knowledge is like a room filled with **furniture**; a man cannot walk about freely in it, and look out of the windows. It is much better to concentrate on a few subjects which interest you - literature, geography, history, science - and deal lightly with others, than **to march sternly and heavily through the whole range of learning like a silly tourist going through a museum** and not missing a single object. If you try to master every [10] subject, you may become very wise, but you will be very inhuman and you will probably lose all your friends. So you must learn to pick and choose, and yet you must learn to browse in a library like a camel browsing in nature. If you watch a camel grazing, you will see that although it is supposed to be one of the most stupid animals in creation, it has at least one of the characteristics of a cultured man - the power to pick and choose. A student looking for mental food in a library should take the [15] camel for a model. The camel wanders about and grazes from here and then there, sometimes from a tree, that is the top shelves of the library; or a bush, the middle shelves; or the grass, the bottom shelves. He bites off a twig, chews a bit and if he likes it, he takes another bite. If he finds it tasteless or bitter, he leaves it and wanders to another tree. Sometimes after trying several leaves and plants, he comes back to the first one. In the end he will probably sit down and chew it over. **Mental** [20] **chewing** over is a very good process for a man as physical chewing over is for a camel. It helps digestion.

**Questions**

11. According to the writer, our attitude towards reading should consist of a/an \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The first sentence says men "must bring to their reading a desire to learn and a power to assimilate", and reading without assimilating is compared to eating without digesting. The attitude is therefore a wish to acquire something real from books, not just entertainment. "Authority", "recognition" and "success in life" are never mentioned. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: longing to gain wisdom and authority
wish to acquire something, not just entertainment

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 11 to 18 above) 12. Francis Bacon advises students to \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: According to Bacon, "a student should read books on those subjects which he is insufficiently acquainted; yet he should be selective in his reading". This is exactly: focus on areas in which they are lacking and read discriminatively. Reading as widely as possible (A) and reading everything one can assimilate (C) contradict the advice to be selective; option D leaves out the first part. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: focus on areas in which they are lacking and read discriminatively
read as much as they can assimilate
select only books that have value

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 11 to 18 above) 13. The word 'furniture' (line 7) is a \_\_\_\_\_\_\_ noun.

*Options as printed:* A) collective   B) common   C) abstract   D) proper
questions.corrige_markdown:
"Furniture" names things, so it is certainly a common noun (not a name such as "Cameroon"), and it is also an uncountable noun that groups many pieces under one word, which some teachers call a collective noun. It is not abstract. Because common (B) and collective (A) are both defensible, this question is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

**Answer: common (B) in the usual grammar sense; collective (A) is also defensible. It is not abstract or proper.**

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 11 to 18 above) 14. When the writer says, '...to march sternly and heavily through the whole range of learning like a silly tourist going through a museum...' (lines 9-10), he is using \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The comparison is introduced by the word "like" (learning is compared to a tourist rushing through a museum), so this is a simile. A metaphor would say the student *is* a tourist, and there is no human quality given to a thing (personification) or exaggeration (hyperbole). **Answer: C.**
themes: O Level English - figures of speech

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 11 to 18 above) 15. The danger in attempting to master every subject is that you \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The writer says "If you try to master every subject, you may become very wise, but you will be very inhuman and you will probably lose all your friends." So the danger is gaining wisdom at the expense of friends. "Jack of all trades" is not in the passage and option D says you keep human feelings, which the passage denies. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: become a jack of all trades
acquire wisdom at the expense of friends
become wise, have human feelings, but lose friends

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 11 to 18 above) 16. According to the writer, a mind overloaded with knowledge leads to \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: A mind overloaded with knowledge "is like a room filled with furniture; a man cannot walk about freely in it". The mind is crowded and cannot move freely, which means confusion. Fulfilment, recognition and wisdom are the opposite of this picture. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 11 to 18 above) 17. What makes a camel similar to cultured man is its ability to \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The camel "has at least one of the characteristics of a cultured man - the power to pick and choose". Picking and choosing is selecting. Wandering about and chewing food are what the camel does, but they are not the shared characteristic. **Answer: D.**
themes: O Level English - synonyms and antonyms

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 11 to 18 above) 18. 'Mental chewing' (lines 20-21), means \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The camel "will probably sit down and chew it over"; for a man, "mental chewing" is therefore to think over what he has read and take time to consider it carefully. It is not eating (A), imagining (C) or simply absorbing information (D). **Answer: B.**
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

choix.texte: considering carefully everything that is eaten

questions.enonce_markdown:
**Passage for questions 19 to 25** (the numbers in square brackets are the line numbers printed in the paper)

**Passage II**

In many places in the world today, the poor are getting poorer while the rich are getting richer, and the programmes of development planning and foreign aid appear to be unable to **reverse this trend**. Nearly all the developing countries have a modern sector, where the patterns of living and working are similar to those in developed countries. But they also have a non-modern sector, where the patterns of living and working are not only unsatisfactory, but in many cases are even getting worse. [5]

What is the typical condition of the poor in developing countries? Their work opportunities are so limited that they cannot work their way out of their situation. They are under-employed, or totally unemployed. When they do find occasional work, their productivity is extremely low. Some of them have land, but often too little land. Many have no land, and no prospect of ever getting any. There is no hope for them in the rural areas, and so they drift into the big cities. But there is no work for them in the big cities either--and of [10] course no housing. All the same, **they flock into the cities** because their chances of finding some work appear to be greater there than in the villages, where such chances are nil. Rural unemployment, then, produces mass migration into the cities. Rural unemployment becomes urban unemployment.

The problem can be stated quite simply: what can be done to promote economic growth in the small towns and villages which still contain about 80 to 90% percent of the population? The primary need is [15] workplaces, **literally millions of workplaces.** No one, of course, would suggest that output per worker is unimportant. But the primary aim cannot be to maximize output per worker; it must be to maximize work opportunities for the unemployed and the under-employed. The poor man's greatest need is the chance to work. Even poorly paid and relatively unproductive work is better than no work at all. It is therefore more important that everybody should produce something, than that a few people should each produce a great [20] deal. And in most developing countries, this can only be achieved by using an appropriate intermediate technology.

**Questions**

19. The expression, 'reverse this trend...' (line 2), as used in the text means \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The trend is that the poor get poorer and the rich get richer. To reverse it is to turn it round so that the situation of the poor improves. "Improve on the situation" is the closest option. Returning to a former state (A) is not what the passage discusses, "consider" is not "reverse", and making the rich poor (D) is not the aim. **Answer: C.**
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

choix.texte: return to the former state of affairs

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 19 to 25 above) 20. According to the passage, the difference between developing countries and developed ones is that, while the former have \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: Developed countries have only a modern sector; developing countries "have a modern sector" and also "a non-modern sector", the two being very different. So the former have two conflicting sectors while the latter have one. Option A is wrong because developed countries do have a modern sector. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: a modern sector, the latter do not have
two conflicting sectors, the latter have one
higher rural unemployment, the latter have higher urban unemployment
appropriate intermediate technology, the latter adopt an inappropriate one

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 19 to 25 above) 21. In the expression "they flock into the city" (line 11), the word flock is used as a/an \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: "They flock" has a subject (they) and "flock" tells what they do, so it is a verb meaning to go together in large numbers. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 19 to 25 above) 22. When the writer says '...literally millions of work places' (line 16), he is suggesting that \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Literally millions" stresses a very large number, so what is suggested is that many millions of jobs should be created. Option A (one million) is too small and B and D speak of appreciating the need or the size of the work force, which is not what the writer says. **Answer: C.**
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

choix.texte: one million jobs must be created
the need for numerous workplaces should be appreciated
many million jobs should be created
the size of the work force should be appreciated

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 19 to 25 above) 23. What the poor man sees as his greatest need is to be \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The text says "The poor man's greatest need is the chance to work." That is: given the chance to work. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 19 to 25 above) 24. According to the writer, the best way of solving the problem of unemployment in developing countries is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The writer says that having everybody produce something "can only be achieved by using an appropriate intermediate technology". So the way he proposes is to use appropriate intermediate technology. "Create more work places" (D) is the aim (the primary need), not the method; B and C are not recommended. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: a few people should produce a great deal

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 19 to 25 above) 25. From the way the writer describes the typical condition of the poor in developing countries, one could conclude that \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The writer says that for the poor "There is no hope for them in the rural areas" and no work in the cities either; they have no land, no work and no housing. The conclusion is that the poor have no hope. Poverty is not called a disease (A), it is not said to be caused by the rich (C), and nothing suggests the problems are temporary (D). **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: rural poverty is caused by the rich
the problems of the poor are temporary

questions.enonce_markdown:
**Section C - Grammar (7½ marks).** Read the instructions for each question or set of questions carefully before answering.

**For numbers 26-38 choose the best answer that completes each sentence.**

26. If this had happened to you, what \_\_\_\_\_\_?
questions.corrige_markdown: "If" + past perfect (had happened) is a third conditional, so the main clause takes "would have" + past participle: "what would you have done?". "Would you do" is a second conditional and "will you do" a first conditional. "Would you have been doing" changes the meaning (an action in progress). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 27. After only a few days of phoning Jessica, she knew my number \_\_\_\_\_\_ heart.
questions.corrige_markdown: The fixed expression is "to know something by heart" (from memory). **Answer: D.**
themes: O Level English - idioms and proverbs

questions.enonce_markdown: 28. Wait here until I \_\_\_\_\_\_ you.
questions.corrige_markdown: After "until" a future event is expressed with the simple present, so "until I call you" is correct. "Will call" and "am going to call" are future forms that are not used after "until". "Call for you" would mean to come and collect you, which does not fit "wait here until I ... you" as naturally. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 29. She danced \_\_\_\_\_ gracefully that the guest of honour promised her a special gift.
questions.corrige_markdown: The pattern "so + adverb + that" expresses result: she danced so gracefully that ... "Very" and "too" cannot be followed by a "that" clause of result, and "more" would need "than". **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 30. Much of the powers of the mayors have been lost. \_\_\_\_\_\_\_, their political influence should not be underestimated.
questions.corrige_markdown: A full clause follows the blank, so we need a connector that works alone: "Even so" (= nevertheless) joins the two sentences. "Although" and "Even though" begin a subordinate clause and need a main clause in the same sentence (here a full stop precedes), and "Even" alone does not link the ideas. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
31. \_\_\_\_\_\_\_ thinks that Eto'o should be made man of the match.

*Options as printed:* A) Neither of us   B) Practically everyone   C) Majority of the players   D) A number of people
questions.corrige_markdown:
The verb "thinks" is singular, so the subject must be singular. "Practically everyone" (B) is singular and makes sense. "Neither of us" (A) is also grammatically singular, and the sentence is acceptable, although the negative meaning is less natural. "Majority of the players" (C) lacks "the" and "a number of people" (D) takes a plural verb. Because A and B are both defensible, this question is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

**Answer: "Practically everyone" (B) is the expected choice; "Neither of us" (A) is also grammatically correct.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 32. Ajara is the captain of the \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ football team.
questions.corrige_markdown: The team belongs to girls (plural), so we use the plural possessive: girls' football team. "Girl" and "girls" alone would not show possession, and "girl's" would mean a team of one girl. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 33. Nina would have passed the examination if she \_\_\_\_\_ all her school needs.
questions.corrige_markdown: The main clause is "would have passed" (third conditional), so the "if" clause takes the past perfect: "had had" (past perfect of the verb have). "Had" is a simple past and "would have had" is not used after "if". **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 34. They will visit their \_\_\_\_\_ next week.
questions.corrige_markdown: In compound nouns such as "daughter-in-law", the plural is formed on the first noun: daughters-in-law. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 35. My uncle took \_\_\_\_\_\_ and \_\_\_\_\_\_ to the market.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Took" has two objects, so we need object forms: "my cousin and me". "I" is a subject form and "myself" is a reflexive that needs the subject to be the same person. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 36. She was surprised to receive a/an \_\_\_\_\_\_ puppy for her birthday.
questions.corrige_markdown: English adjectives follow the order opinion, size, age: cute (opinion) little (size) eight-week-old (age) puppy. The other options break this order. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 37. She sent the child to play \_\_\_\_\_\_ she could sleep.
questions.corrige_markdown: "So that" introduces a purpose: she sent the child out so that she could sleep. "Then" and "since" do not give a purpose, and "while" would mean at the same time as. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 38. It wasn't an accident. The window was broken on purpose, \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ ?
questions.corrige_markdown: The statement is positive ("was broken"), so the question tag is negative and uses the same auxiliary: "wasn't it?". **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
**39. Choose the correct form of reported speech.**

"I will inform her that I saw you." She said that she \_\_\_\_\_\_ her that she \_\_\_\_\_\_ me.
questions.corrige_markdown: In reported speech after "said", "will" becomes "would" and the simple past "saw" becomes the past perfect "had seen": She said that she would inform her that she had seen me. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: **40. Choose the sentence that is correctly punctuated.**
questions.corrige_markdown: "Njie Clinton" is extra information about the centre forward (an appositive), so it is set off by a pair of commas, one before and one after: "The centre forward, Njie Clinton, scored a goal." Options B and D have only one comma, and A has none. **Answer: C.**
themes: O Level English - spelling and punctuation

choix.texte: The centre forward Njie Clinton scored a goal.
The centre forward, Njie Clinton scored a goal.
The centre forward, Njie Clinton, scored a goal.
The centre forward Njie Clinton, scored a goal.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**Section D - Vocabulary (5 marks).** Read the instructions for each question or set of questions carefully before answering.

**For numbers 41-45 choose the answer that best completes each sentence.**

41. Ten men went hunting; eight came back. Therefore, \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ came.
questions.corrige_markdown: Eight out of ten is a large majority, so "most" of them came back. "Some" and "several" suggest a smaller or vaguer number, and "many" does not show the proportion of the ten. **Answer: C.**
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 42. Teachers are advised not to \_\_\_\_\_ students.
questions.corrige_markdown: The verb that fits is "beat" (hit repeatedly as punishment). "Bit" and "bite" would not make sense here, and "bid" means to offer a price. **Answer: B.**
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 43. Remember to \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ your medicine before you go to bed.
questions.corrige_markdown: The usual collocation is "take your medicine". "Drink" only suits liquids, "swallow" describes only the physical act and "consume" is too formal for a prescription. **Answer: B.**
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 44. Candidates scoring marks above 80% are \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ for this scholarship.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Eligible" means qualified or allowed to receive something because one meets the conditions. "Worthy" would need "of", "competent" means able and "permissible" is for things, not people. **Answer: D.**
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 45. The jealous girls made very \_\_\_\_\_\_ approving remarks about her good results.
questions.corrige_markdown: The prefix that gives "the opposite of approving" is "dis": disapproving. "Un-", "in-" and "il-" cannot be added to "approving". **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
**For numbers 46-48 choose the answer that best explains the meaning of the underlined word or phrase (shown in bold here).**

46. She **went through fire** after her husband died.
questions.corrige_markdown: "To go through fire" is an idiom meaning to suffer a lot, to pass through severe hardship. **Answer: C.**
themes: O Level English - idioms and proverbs

questions.enonce_markdown: 47. Those who stole the money **should be brought to book**.
questions.corrige_markdown: "To be brought to book" means to be made to explain and answer for one's actions, that is, to be held to account. **Answer: D.**
themes: O Level English - idioms and proverbs

questions.enonce_markdown: 48. A fashion shop can be a **lucrative** business.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Lucrative" means producing a lot of money, so the best explanation is "profitable". **Answer: D.**
themes: O Level English - synonyms and antonyms
O Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown:
**For numbers 49 and 50 choose the answer that gives the opposite of the underlined word (shown in bold here).**

49. Peter is fond of asking **pertinent** questions.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Pertinent" means relevant to the matter, so its opposite is "irrelevant". **Answer: C.**
themes: O Level English - synonyms and antonyms

questions.enonce_markdown: 50. Mary felt **nervous** when she attended the interview.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Nervous" means anxious and tense, so the opposite is "relaxed". "Anxious" and "worried" are synonyms and "cautious" is not an opposite. **Answer: B.**
themes: O Level English - synonyms and antonyms
